content: The Drug Susceptibility Testing (DST) is a critical process for determining the effectiveness of anti-tuberculosis (TB) drugs against Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). The External Review Group (ERG) and the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND) are key organizations involved in advancing diagnostic tools for TB. First-line Line Probe Assays (FL-LPA) and second-line Line Probe Assays (SL-LPA) are molecular diagnostic tools used to detect TB and drug resistance. The Fujifilm SILVAMP TB LAM assay is a diagnostic test that detects lipoarabinomannan (LAM), a mycobacterial antigen, in urine samples, particularly useful for people living with HIV (PLHIV). The Guideline Development Group (GDG) employs the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach to assess the quality of evidence and formulate recommendations. This system ensures transparency, comprehensiveness, and practicality in developing global health guidelines. The World Health Organization (WHO) has consolidated its TB diagnostic guidelines to simplify access for healthcare providers, national TB programs, and policymakers. Advanced HIV disease is defined as a CD4 cell count of less than 200 cells/mm³ or the presence of a WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 event. All children under five years of age with HIV are considered to have advanced disease. Age groups are categorized as follows: adults are 15 years and older, adolescents are 10–19 years, and children are under 10 years. The WHO's End TB Strategy emphasizes early diagnosis and universal drug susceptibility testing (DST) to combat TB effectively. The traditional light microscopy method for TB diagnosis, developed over a century ago, has been surpassed by newer technologies that detect mycobacterial antigens or DNA. These include nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), which are highly sensitive and specific for detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) DNA and drug resistance mutations. The WHO has endorsed a range of diagnostic technologies, including automated NAATs, lateral flow urine LAM assays, and line probe assays (LPAs). Automated NAATs, such as Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, are widely used for detecting TB and rifampicin resistance. LPAs, which are more complex, can detect resistance to a broader range of first-line and second-line anti-TB drugs and provide mutation-specific data. These tests are designed for reference laboratory settings and are particularly relevant in high TB burden countries. The lateral flow urine LAM assay is a point-of-care test that detects the LAM antigen in urine. While its sensitivity and specificity are suboptimal for general TB diagnosis, it is particularly effective for diagnosing TB in individuals co-infected with HIV. The WHO has recommended its use in specific populations of presumptive TB patients. The WHO has also evaluated three new classes of diagnostic technologies: moderate complexity automated NAATs for detecting TB and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, low complexity automated NAATs for detecting resistance to isoniazid and second-line anti-TB agents, and high complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs for detecting pyrazinamide resistance. These technologies represent significant advancements in TB diagnostics, enabling rapid and accurate detection of TB and drug resistance. The WHO's consolidated guidelines on TB diagnostics aim to streamline recommendations from multiple previously published guidelines and include updates on new technologies evaluated in 2020–2021. These guidelines are essential for achieving global TB targets, such as diagnosing and treating 40 million people with TB between 2018 and 2022. The focus is on scaling up the use of sensitive diagnostic tools to increase the proportion of bacteriologically confirmed TB cases and ensure appropriate treatment regimens are initiated promptly.
